summaries.gardner: PepsiCo is the opposite of a Rule Breaker: a mature leader in slow-growing snack and soda markets, with shares down about 13% over the past year and a stock widely described as cheap rather than overvalued. It does score on brand strength and household recognition, but lacks the emerging-industry, top-dog-in-a-new-market and momentum traits Gardner looks for.
summaries.buffett: PepsiCo has many Buffett-style traits: simple products, enduring brands such as Lay's, Doritos and Gatorade, 54 straight years of dividend increases and free cash flow close to net income. Against that, operating margin has fallen from 14.3% to 12.2% over five years, debt of about $51.9 billion is high relative to equity, and a value-minded buyer would want evidence the North American business has stabilised.
summaries.munger: Munger would recognise a durable consumer franchise with scale in distribution that is hard to replicate, and few ways for the whole business to fail. He would also note the stresses: price-driven volume losses, GLP-1 and health trends, and an activist pushing for change, so this is a good business at a fair price rather than a great business at a bargain.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms PepsiCo is a stalwart that has turned into a mild turnaround story, with a simple story (cut prices and costs to win back snack volume). Its P/E of about 15.5 times forward earnings is well above its expected EPS growth of a few percent, so it does not pass his P/E-to-growth test, and it is heavily covered by Wall Street.
summaries.fisher: PepsiCo is unusually strong at selling and distribution and keeps launching products (Doritos Protein, Simply NKD snacks, prebiotic cola), but much of its newer growth was bought (poppi, Siete) and margins have been falling. It fits Fisher's points on sales organisation and management depth better than his points on long-run profit-margin improvement and growth potential.
summaries.graham: PepsiCo passes Graham's size, earnings-stability and dividend-record tests (54 consecutive annual dividend increases, EPS up 63% from $3.67 in 2015 to $6.00 in 2025). It fails his price tests: about 20 times average three-year earnings and a price-to-book near 8, and its current ratio of about 0.85 is below his preference.
summaries.thiel: PepsiCo has no proprietary technology and did not start as a monopoly of a small new market; its strengths are distribution and brands built over decades. On Thiel's seven questions it scores only on distribution and durability, so it is not the kind of business he looks for.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on companies riding big technology shifts with improving operating efficiency at a sensible price. PepsiCo is cutting costs and SKUs under Elliott's influence, but its revenue grows only mid-single digits and it is not exposed to AI or other platform shifts.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and rising estimates; PepsiCo has the reverse, having cut 2026 core EPS growth guidance to +2.5% to +3.5% in October 2026. Possible catalysts exist (price cuts lifting volume, cost cuts, activist pressure), but the setup lacks the strong momentum and estimate revisions he favours.
summaries.smith: PepsiCo meets parts of Terry Smith's test: resilient consumer brands, high gross margin of about 54%, solid cash conversion and a return on invested capital near 20%. But the return relies partly on heavy debt, margins and organic growth have weakened, so it is a good company whose quality has slipped rather than a clear Fundsmith-style compounder.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, PepsiCo has a reasonable earnings yield (EBIT to enterprise value of roughly 7% on trailing figures) and a good return on capital, helped by an asset-light-ish snack business. It would likely rank in the middle to upper half of large caps rather than at the top.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, talented and honest managers, and great reinvestment opportunities. PepsiCo has the first leg, an adequate second leg, but limited high-return reinvestment: capital spending is kept below 5% of revenue and recent growth came from acquisitions at full prices.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple businesses in temporary trouble with little downside. PepsiCo's North American volume slump and six-year-low share price fit the 'temporary setback' idea and permanent loss looks unlikely, but the stock is not cheap enough to offer the large discount to value his 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' approach requires.
summaries.wood: PepsiCo has no exposure to Cathie Wood's innovation platforms (AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain, multiomics) and its market cannot grow many times over in five years. It falls outside ARK's disruptive-innovation framework.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating businesses with strong moats, often where an activist catalyst can fix underperformance. PepsiCo fits much of that profile, and Elliott's 2025 stake shows activists see fixable issues, though its balance sheet is more leveraged than Ackman typically prefers.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model asks whether a company passes its scale savings back to customers. PepsiCo's 2026 price cuts of up to 15%, funded by productivity, are a step in that direction, but for years it did the opposite, raising prices faster than costs, so it is not a natural Nomad holding.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine looked for huge, fast-growing markets created by technology shifts. PepsiCo serves huge but mature markets with no technological disruption, so it fits his approach poorly.
summaries.nash: PepsiCo fails most of Tom Nash's hard filters: revenue growth is about 5-6%, operating margin is below 20%, debt far exceeds cash and the five-year share price return trails the S&P 500. It scores well on profitability, low short interest, high institutional ownership and simplicity, but its total score (about 55 of 130) is well below his 75-point bar.

momentum.evidence: The shares closed at $131.49 on October 16, 2026, down about 13% over 52 weeks, after hitting $125.10 on October 5, 2026, their lowest level since April 2020.

g4.evidence: Chairman and CEO Ramon Laguarta is an experienced operator, and activist Elliott Investment Management took a roughly $4 billion stake in September 2025, but the activist is there because results have disappointed.

g6.evidence: Commentators describe PepsiCo as cheap, noting a forward P/E near 14-15 times, the lowest in five years, rather than calling it overvalued.

simple.evidence: PepsiCo makes and sells chips, sodas, sports drinks and oats such as Lay's, Doritos, Pepsi, Gatorade and Quaker, a business any generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from FY2020 to FY2025, the company has been profitable throughout, and it raised its dividend for the 54th consecutive year in 2026.

integrity.evidence: Management has been candid about North American weakness and cut guidance in October 2026, and PepsiCo has been named one of Ethisphere's World's Most Ethical Companies for 20 years, but the CEO is also chairman and key changes (price cuts, 20% SKU reduction) came after activist pressure.

b6.evidence: Recent deals (Siete $1.2 billion, poppi $1.95 billion, $585 million for Celsius preferred stock) follow the industry trend toward better-for-you brands, but they are modest in size relative to a $94 billion revenue company.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 20% (StockAnalysis, October 2026), but return on equity of over 50% is inflated by heavy borrowing, with total liabilities of $86,852m against equity of $20,547m at the end of FY2025.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 operating cash flow of $12,087m minus capital spending of $4,415m gave $7,672m of free cash flow, about 93% of net income of $8,240m.

b10.evidence: EPS grew from $3.67 in 2015 to $6.00 in 2025, but the share price is at a six-year low, so retained earnings and debt-funded growth have added less market value than a Buffett test would want.

safety.evidence: At $131.49 the stock trades at about 15.5 times forward earnings with low-single-digit growth, and a conservative cash-flow valuation does not show a clear discount to value.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 15.5 and a free-cash-flow yield near 5.8% (StockAnalysis TTM) are reasonable for a quality staple, but growth is low and 2026 core EPS is guided up only 2.5% to 3.5%.

mu5.evidence: With dozens of major brands sold in more than 200 countries and about 58% food, 42% beverages, there are few realistic paths to outright failure; the main risks are slow erosion from health trends and private label.

reinvest.evidence: PepsiCo targets capital spending below 5% of revenue and returns most cash ($7.9 billion of dividends and $1.0 billion of buybacks planned for 2026), so high-return internal reinvestment is limited.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic stalwart with a simple turnaround story: cut prices and costs in North America to win back snack and drink volume.

ly3.evidence: The P/E of about 15.5 times forward earnings is far above expected EPS growth of about 2.5% to 3.5% for 2026.

runway.evidence: International snacks (EMEA up 9% and Asia Pacific Foods up 9% organically in Q3 2026) and functional drinks offer growth, but total revenue growth is expected to stay in the low-to-mid single digits.

ly7.evidence: Weighted diluted shares fell slowly from 1,392m in FY2020 to 1,367m in Q3 2026, but buybacks are only $1.0 billion a year and no meaningful insider buying was found.

ly8.evidence: PepsiCo is followed by about 24 analysts and is one of the most widely held consumer staples, so it is not overlooked.

fi2.evidence: PepsiCo keeps launching new products as old ones mature, such as Doritos Protein, Simply NKD Doritos and Cheetos without artificial colors, and a prebiotic Pepsi cola, and it added poppi and Siete.

fi3.evidence: Innovation helped Frito-Lay regain volume share in 2026 (year-to-date organic volume and share up in North America convenient foods), but many of its fastest-growing brands were acquired rather than developed in-house.

fi4.evidence: Retailers ranked PepsiCo the No. 1 supplier in the Kantar PoweRanking for 2025, the 10th consecutive year, reflecting its direct-store-delivery sales force.

longterm.evidence: Management is investing in price cuts, marketing and innovation at the cost of near-term margins, but the moves were prompted by falling volumes and activist pressure rather than a long-standing long-term philosophy.

gr1.evidence: PepsiCo had $93,925m of FY2025 revenue and a market value of about $179 billion in October 2026.

ni10.evidence: PepsiCo reported positive net income in every year of the last decade, from $5,452m in 2015 to $8,240m in 2025.

gr4.evidence: PepsiCo raised its dividend for the 54th consecutive year in 2026, to an annualised $5.92 per share.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $3.67 in 2015 to $6.00 in 2025, an increase of about 63%.

gr6.evidence: At $131.49 the shares trade at about 20 times average diluted EPS of the last three years ($6.56, $6.95 and $6.00).

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 22 on FY2025 EPS times a price-to-book of about 8 (market value about $179 billion versus equity of $22,487m) gives roughly 175, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: PepsiCo's advantage is brands and distribution, not proprietary technology that is ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: Demand is shifting toward protein, prebiotic and less-processed products, which PepsiCo is chasing with poppi, Siete and Simply NKD, but GLP-1 drugs and health concerns are a headwind for its core chips and sodas.

th3.evidence: PepsiCo is already a $94 billion company in mature markets; it is not expanding out from a dominant share of a small new market.

team.evidence: The management team is experienced and global, but under Laguarta operating margin fell from 14.3% (FY2020) to 12.2% (FY2025) and an activist investor took a stake to push for change.

th5.evidence: PepsiCo's direct-store-delivery network and bottling system put its products in stores in more than 200 countries and territories, a distribution advantage it also rents to partners such as Celsius.

durable.evidence: Brands like Lay's, Doritos, Pepsi and Gatorade have lasted decades and snacks and drinks are hard to disrupt technologically, though health trends may slowly shrink some categories.

th7.evidence: PepsiCo competes in well-understood markets where its opportunities are visible to all major rivals.

trend.evidence: PepsiCo is not a leading beneficiary of AI, cloud or another platform shift; it uses AI internally but sells snacks and drinks.

dr1.evidence: In October 2026 PepsiCo cut 2026 core EPS growth guidance to +2.5% to +3.5% from the low end of +5% to +7%, pushing estimates down.

dr2.evidence: Price cuts, a 20% reduction in US products and new cost savings could lift North American volumes and margins by 2027-2028, but this recovery plan is already widely discussed.

dr4.evidence: Lower interest rates would ease the cost of about $51.9 billion of debt, but squeezed consumers trading down to private label hurt volumes.

dr6.evidence: Potential drivers include volume recovery from the 2026 price cuts, cost cuts, international snack growth and further changes pushed by Elliott, but none is certain.

dr7.evidence: With guidance being cut and growth low, the case does not support the very high conviction needed for a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 54.1% in FY2025 ($50,859m gross profit on $93,925m revenue), high for a food and beverage company.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $10.5 billion on a market value of about $179 billion gives a free-cash-flow yield near 5.8% (StockAnalysis, October 2026), reasonable for a stable staple.

gb2.evidence: Enterprise value of about $220 billion is roughly 14 times trailing operating profit (EBIT yield about 7%), reasonable but not high.

pa2.evidence: The North American volume slump after years of price rises looks partly fixable through price cuts and cost savings, but GLP-1 drugs and health trends may be more lasting.

pa4.evidence: PepsiCo's diverse portfolio, $12 billion of yearly operating cash flow and 54-year dividend-growth record make permanent loss of capital unlikely, even if returns disappoint.

wo1.evidence: PepsiCo does not lead in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Snack and drink unit costs are not falling rapidly with volume; input costs and tariffs pressured profits in 2026.

wo3.evidence: PepsiCo does not combine disruptive innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market grows at low single digits and cannot become many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: PepsiCo is exposed to commodity costs (potatoes, corn, oils, sugar, aluminum), tariffs, currency swings and interest costs on about $51.9 billion of debt.

ns1.evidence: In 2026 PepsiCo used productivity savings to fund price cuts of up to 15% on Lay's, Doritos and Cheetos, but for years before it raised prices faster than costs.

ns4.evidence: Its brands and distribution should endure, but it is not clear its position in 10-20 years will be stronger, given health trends and soda share losses.

va2.evidence: Snacks and soft drinks satisfy everyday cravings rather than solve a large, painful problem.

tn1.evidence: PepsiCo is an established food and beverage company, not one built for AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees PepsiCo as a slow-growing snacks and drinks company, which is what it is; there is no hidden transformation.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap US company and not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn9.evidence: It hits instant kills: more debt than cash, and an operating margin of 12.2% in FY2025, below 20%.

tn10.evidence: PepsiCo's FY2025 10-K flags food, ingredient and marketing regulation, packaging laws and taxes as risks, though no single case threatens the business.

tn11.evidence: PepsiCo provides branded snacks and drinks that help retailers and restaurants satisfy shoppers' everyday cravings, and charges per unit sold through stores, bottlers and food service.
